question: Organophosphates irreversibly inhibit acetylcholinesterase. Which set of features accurately describes the consequence of excess ACh accumulation at muscarinic receptors?

answers.text: Bradycardia, miosis, excessive salivation, bronchospasm, and urinary incontinence

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Excess ACh at muscarinic receptors produces the SLUDGE/DUMBELS toxidrome: bradycardia (M2 on SA node), miosis (M3 on sphincter pupillae), salivation and lacrimation (M3 on glands), bronchospasm (M3 on bronchial smooth muscle), and urinary incontinence (M3 on detrusor).

answers.text: Tachycardia, mydriasis, dry mouth, and urinary retention

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. These are features of muscarinic antagonism (anticholinergic toxidrome) — the exact opposite. Tachycardia, mydriasis, dry mouth, and urinary retention occur with atropine excess, not ACh excess.

answers.text: Skeletal muscle paralysis only — muscarinic receptors are not affected by AChE inhibitors

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. AChE inhibition affects ALL cholinergic synapses — both nicotinic (NMJ → fasciculations then paralysis) and muscarinic (autonomic → SLUDGE). Muscarinic effects are often the most immediately dangerous (bronchospasm, bronchorrhoea).

answers.text: Hypertension and diaphoresis consistent with sympathetic activation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The dominant muscarinic picture is parasympathetic overactivation: bradycardia, hypotension, miosis, and secretory excess. Diaphoresis can occur via nicotinic stimulation of sweat glands, but it does not define the muscarinic syndrome.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember SLUDGE: Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Defaecation, GI cramps, Emesis. Add Bradycardia, Bronchospasm, and Miosis. This is the muscarinic excess picture — the opposite of atropine toxicity.
Well done. The SLUDGE/DUMBELS mnemonic captures the muscarinic toxidrome — recognising it instantly is the first step in OPC poisoning management.
